```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr)

hunter_dir <- "/Volumes/HoehnK/Hunter"

chinmay_dir <- "/Volumes/HoehnK/Chinmay"

sirap_dir <- file.path(hunter_dir, "spatial_bcr_tcr_package", "SIRAP")

sample_id <- "KH02"
```

Starting with RAD-processed output for Visium thymus (igblast_bcr.tsv)
slice 2.  We'll take a full tour of SIRAP and the major functionality.

# Start with the RAD/IgBLAST output

The starting BCR table is the direct IgBLAST output made after RAD
demultiplexing.

The full data is like 30G, so we're only loading 10k sequences to see how the processing
works. Once we have the data, we run `extractSpatialBarcodes`, which is just a convenience
function that extracts a barcode from a column (sequence_id_col) using a regex expression
(regex) and then makes a new column (barcode_col).

```{r read-rad-output}
raw_bcr_path <- file.path(
  chinmay_dir,
  "101724_KH02_compiled_out",
  "igblast_data",
  "igblast_bcr_10k.tsv"
)

# This is a 24 GB read-level table, so we just get 10k sequences
raw_bcrs <- data.table::fread(
  raw_bcr_path,
  data.table = FALSE,
  nThread = nproc,
  showProgress = FALSE
)

raw_bcrs <- extractSpatialBarcodes(
  raw_bcrs,
  sequence_id_col = "sequence_id",
  barcode_col = "barcode",
  regex = "\\|barcode:([ACGT]{16})(?:\\||$)"
)

raw_bcrs$sample_id <- sample_id

raw_bcrs %>%
  count(locus, productive, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(10)
```

Now we'll filter the spAIRR data with `filterSpatialAirr()`, which is another convenience
function to do the sort of filtering we've always done with spAIRR data. We have options to
filter for locus, min v, j, junction length, productivity, min consensus count, and we point
towards the spatial barcode column (technically optional argument).
We don't do it here, but we can also filter for max
opening gap in the seqeuence alignment column (max_opening_gap), and we can also add a
"full_id" (add_full_id) which combines the sequence_id and the spatial barcode columns.

Then I made another convenience function that plots the v, j, and junction lengths,
`plotLengthQc()`.  That's all it does, but we've often used those plots, so I figured why not.
spatialReceptorSummary is similar, it's a convenience function that prints the number of
sequences, spatial barcodes, loci, and productive sequences.

```{r filter-rad-output}
raw_igh <- filterSpatialAirr(
  raw_bcrs,
  loci = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 100,
  min_j_length = 10,
  min_junction_length = 1,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = 2,
  barcode_col = "barcode"
) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(barcode),
    !is.na(sequence_alignment),
    sequence_alignment != ""
  )

plotLengthQc(raw_igh, bin_width = 5, title = "KH02 Length QC")
spatialReceptorSummary(raw_igh, barcode_col = "barcode")
```

# Presto Pipeline - processSpatialSample()

Before running `processSpatialSample()` and doing the major processing, we'll convert the
raw_igh dataframe into a fasta file using dowser's `dfToFasta()` function. We'll also pretend
that we want to carry a c_call column through the processing, so we add that to the sequence
id so that it gets written to the fasta header. We're not actually going to run this locally
because it takes a while.

`processSpatialSample()` takes the spAIRR processing pipeline we made and wraps it up in a
single R function.  It takes in a fasta file (and a lot of arguments for the different steps)
and returns a list of paths to the processed output.  This function is a wrapper around
* `ClusterSets.py set` groups reads within each spatial barcode `cluster_field`, the requested identity threshold `identity`, and vsearch. FASTA header delimiters are specified by `delimiters`.
* `ParseHeaders.py merge` is used to write a new field into the headers that combines the spatial barcode and the cluster id (provided with parse_fields). These are combined using `parse_act` (default cat) and written to a new header field `parse_key`.  Uses `delimiters` to specify the FASTA header delimiters.
* `AlignSets.py muscle` aligns reads within each `parse_key` group created by `ParseHeaders`. Takes `muscle_exec` as the path to the muscle aligner (https://github.com/rcedgar/muscle). Optionally logs results to `align_log`. Uses `delimiters` to specify the FASTA header delimiters.
* `BuildConsensus.py` creates consensus sequences within each `parse_key` group. `consensus_min_count` specifies the minimum number of sequences needed to define a valid consensus sequence, and `consensus_freq` specifies the fraction of character occurrences under which an ambiguous character is assigned. Optionally logs results to `consensus_log`. If there are additional fields in the FASTA header that should be carried forward and copied to the consensus file, `consensus_copy_fields` specifies the field names and `consensus_copy_action` specifies how to copy them (majority, first, last, or all).
* `AssignGenes.py igblast` assigns V(D)J gene annotations using IgBLAST. Takes either `ig` or `tr` as the argument to `receptor` (for bcr/tcr respectively). Takes `organism` as the argument to specify the species (e.g., human, mouse, etc.). `igblast_base` specifies the path to the IgBLAST installation, and `igblast_exec` can be provided if the igblast executable is not located in [`igblast_base`]/bin/igblastn.
* `MakeDb.py igblast` converts IgBLAST output to an AIRR-style TSV using the specified IMGT germline reference `germline_glob`.


```{r process-spatial-sample, eval=FALSE}
presto_input_dir <- file.path(walkthrough_dir, "processing_input")
presto_output_dir <- file.path(walkthrough_dir, "processing_output")
dir.create(presto_input_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(presto_output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

raw_igh <- fread(file.path(presto_input_dir, "filtered_igh.tsv"), data.table = FALSE)

raw_igh$c_call_for_header <- ifelse(
  is.na(raw_igh$c_call) | raw_igh$c_call == "",
  "NA",
  raw_igh$c_call
)
raw_igh$seq_id_c_call <- paste0(
  raw_igh$sequence_id,
  "|c_call_og:",
  raw_igh$c_call_for_header
)

presto_input_fasta <- file.path(presto_input_dir, "filtered_igh.fasta")
dowser::dfToFasta(
  raw_igh,
  file = presto_input_fasta,
  id = "seq_id_c_call",
  seq = "sequence_alignment"
)

processed_paths <- processSpatialSample(
  input_fasta = presto_input_fasta,
  output_dir = presto_output_dir,
  receptor = "ig",
  identity = 1.0,
  consensus_freq = 0.8,
  germline_glob = file.path(
    hunter_dir,
    "germlines/imgt/human/vdj/imgt_human_IG*.fasta"
  ),
  igblast_base = "~/software/igblast",
  muscle_exec = "~/software/muscle3.8.31_i86linux64",
  nproc = nproc,
  cluster_field = "barcode",
  delimiters = "'|' ':' ','",
  parse_fields = c("BARCODE", "CLUSTER"),
  parse_key = "BARCODECLUSTER",
  parse_act = "cat",
  consensus_min_count = 2,
  consensus_copy_fields = "C_CALL_OG",
  consensus_copy_action = "majority"
)
```

Now that we have the processed BCRs, we'll do a little more filtering with
`filterSpatialAirr()`, which is a convenience function that filters for v gene length (`min_v_length`), j gene length (`min_j_length`), junction length (`min_junction_length`), locus (`locus`), minimum consensus count (`min_consensus_count`), maximum gap to start the sequence - spAIRR data can often be very ................AGC at the beginning of sequences (`max_opening_gap`). We also specify the `sequence_alignment_col`, `sequence_id_col`, and `barcode_col`. To make things easier later and ensure we have unique identifiers for mixed datasets, we can also request a full_id be made by combining the sequence id and the spatial barcode with `add_full_id`, and we can name this column with `full_id_barcode_key`. How much we really needed this function I'm not sure, but I did this sort of filtering enough that I was okay with having an easy way to do it in the package. Prior to using `filterSpatialAirr()`, we extract the spatial barcode from the `sequence_id` column with `extractSpatialBarcodes()`, which is just a quick function that pulls a regex from a column and puts it in a new column.  We also add a `consensus_count` column and receptor type column.

```{r read-processed-bcrs}
processed_bcr_path <- file.path(
  thymus_dir,
  "sirap_visium_processing",
  sample_id,
  "bcr",
  "presto_output",
  paste0(
    "filtered_igh_ident_1.0_barcode_cluster_freq_0.8_cluster-pass_",
    "reheader_align-pass_consensus-pass_igblast_db-pass.tsv"
  )
)

processed_bcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(processed_bcr_path)
processed_bcrs %>% select(sequence_id, sequence_alignment)

processed_bcrs <- processed_bcrs %>%
  extractSpatialBarcodes(
    sequence_id_col = "sequence_id",
    barcode_col = "barcode_10x",
    regex = "^[ACGT]{16}",
    suffix = "-1"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    consensus_count = as.integer(str_match(sequence_id, "CONSCOUNT:([0-9]+)")[, 2]),
    receptor_type = "BCR"
  )
processed_bcrs %>% select(sequence_id, barcode_10x, consensus_count, receptor_type) %>% 
  head()

processed_bcrs <- filterSpatialAirr(
  processed_bcrs,
  loci = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 100,
  min_j_length = 10,
  min_junction_length = 1,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = 2,
  barcode_col = "barcode_10x"
)

spatialReceptorSummary(processed_bcrs, barcode_col = "barcode_10x")
summary(processed_bcrs$consensus_count)
```

# Load the spatial object

```{r load-seurat}
seurat_path <- file.path(
  thymus_dir,
  "data/240814_Visium/Intermediates/51T002-M5b/thy2_b_t_processed_seurat.rds"
)

mg_thymus_slice2 <- readRDS(seurat_path)
mg_thymus_slice2
```

# Make a SIRAP object

A SIRAP object is our native S3 object for spAIRR data.  At base level, it consists of a 
spatial seurat object (`spatial`) and an airr-style receptor table (`receptors`). When we
create a SIRAP object, we pass a barcode column (`barcode_col`) that corresponds to the 
barcodes in the Seurat object, i.e., the column names in the GEX matrix. Optional arguments
for a clone ID column (`clone_col`), a locus column (`locus_col`), and a consensus count
column (`count_col`) exist too.  The SIRAP object also has a list of metadata (`metadata`)
and a list of analyses (`analyses`).  

The metadata list stores common receptor column names and other information about the sample.
It includes the `dataset` ("mg_thymus_slice2"), the `sample_id` ("KH02"), and important columns from the receptors dataframe `receptor_fields`. `receptor_fields` is itself a list that includes the `barcode` column name ("barcode_10x"), the `image` column name (currently NULL), the `image` and `sample` column names, the `clone` column name ("clone_id"), the `locus` column name ("locus"), and the `count` column name ("consensus_count"). The idea here is that sometimes the receptor data has different column names (like clone_family_id in the original Engblom tonsil data), and we want to make the SIRAP object easily respect those.

When working with a SIRAP object, we can use `spatialObject()` to get the Seurat object,
`receptorTable()` to get the receptor table, and `listAnalyses()` to see what analyses have
been run and stored in the object.  We can also use `summary()` to get a quick overview. When
we want to run a function on the SIRAP spatial data, we can use `withSpatial()` to pass the
spatial data to a function and return the result.  We can do the same but update the SIRAP
spatial data with `updateSpatial()`. The same pattern exists for the receptor table with 
`withReceptors()` and `updateReceptors()`.  Finally, we can store the results of an analysis 
in the SIRAP object with `setAnalysis()` and retrieve it with `getAnalysis()`.  We can also 
use a stored analysis in a function with `withAnalysis` and update a stored analysis with 
`updateAnalysis()`.

```{r make-preclone-sirap-object}
mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- createSIRAP(
  spatial = mg_thymus_slice2,
  receptors = processed_bcrs,
  barcode_col = "barcode_10x",
  clone_col = NULL,
  locus_col = "locus",
  count_col = "consensus_count",
  metadata = list(dataset = dataset, sample_id = sample_id)
)

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap
summary(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)
spatialReceptorSummary(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)

spatialObject(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)
receptorTable(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap) %>% head()
listAnalyses(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)
```

# Check for identical sequences in neighboring spots

SIRAP can collapse the same exact sequence observed in neighboring spots with
`collapseIdenticalNeighbors()`. Input is a SIRAP object, so the
function uses the receptor barcode field recorded in the object and pulls
coordinates from the stored Seurat object.

We know that spatial sequencing data suffers from bleed between spots, so we
don't necessarily want to count the same exact sequence in neighboring spots
unless we're quite sure that this represents distinct cells. I wouldn't
recommend running this function on standard 10X Visium data, since each 55um
spot has multiple cells and spots are 100um away from each other. Absolutely use
it with Visium HD data.

`collapseIdenticalNeighbors()` estimates the neighbor distance threshold from all tissue
coordinates, so it's very important to get `num_neighbors_non_boundary` correct. For standard
Visium data, this is 6 because it's a hex grid, for Visium HD data, this is 8 because it's a 
continuous lawn. It estimates the spatial neighbor distance from a downsampled version of the
tissue coordinates using RANN's `knn()` to do nearest neighbor searching with a kd-tree. Then
we take all of the unique distances and do a kernel smoothing and use the first local minimum
as the distance threshold (extremely similar to the threshold selection in
hierarchicalClones). 

Then we filter to spots with observed receptor sequences and build an undirected adjacency 
graph from those spots using the distance threshold to define adjacency (i.e., neighbors). 
Then, for every unique sequence, we look in each component of of the graph and find connected
spots that have the same sequence represented.For each component, we choose one 
representative spot. First pick the row with the highest consensus_count, if there is a tie, 
choose the spot closest to the component centroid. If there is still a tie, pick one at 
random.

```{r neighboring-sequence-diagnostic}
image_name <- Images(spatialObject(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap))[1]

neighbor_collapsed_sirap <- collapseIdenticalNeighbors(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  num_neighbors_non_boundary = 6
)

neighbor_collapsed_bcrs <- receptorTable(neighbor_collapsed_sirap)

tibble(
  version = c("original Visium table", "neighbor-collapsed diagnostic"),
  n_sequences = c(nrow(receptorTable(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)), nrow(neighbor_collapsed_bcrs)),
  n_spots = c(
    n_distinct(receptorTable(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)$barcode_10x),
    n_distinct(neighbor_collapsed_bcrs$barcode_10x)
  )
)

# Everything below continues with mg_thymus_slice2_sirap, not neighbor_collapsed_sirap.
plotReceptors(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  group_col = "receptor_type",
  values = "BCR",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  receptor_size = 1.5,
  receptor_alpha = 0.5,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  title = "All spots",
  show_receptor_legend = FALSE
)
plotReceptors(
  neighbor_collapsed_sirap,
  group_col = "receptor_type",
  values = "BCR",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  receptor_size = 1.5,
  receptor_alpha = 0.5,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  title = "Identical neighbor collapsed spots",
  show_receptor_legend = FALSE
)
```

# Build BCR clones

I made functions that allow us to use external functions (i.e., dowser, seurat stuff) that 
interact with the spatial or receptors slot in a SIRAP object. The `withReceptors()` function
passes the receptor table to any function and returns that function's result. Its
corresponding partner function `updateReceptors()` sticks the result back into the SIRAP
object's receptors slot. Both functions take all additional arguments used for the functions 
that we're calling. For example, if we want to build clones using the receptor sequences
in the SIRAP object, we could do this:

```{r sample-only-clone-example}
sample_only_clones <- withReceptors(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  cell_id = "sequence_id",
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = nproc
)

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- updateReceptors(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  cell_id = "sequence_id",
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = nproc
)
```

Note that updateReceptors automatically updates the SIRAP metadata with the clone column name
(if it's clone_id), and otherwise we can pass `receptor_fields = list(clone ="new_clone_col")` to `updateReceptors` and it'll update the metadata accordingly.

# Plot expression and BCRs

We use `spatialExpressionPlot()` to plot gene expression and `plotReceptors()` to plot
BCRs/TCRs. 

`spatialExpressionPlot()` takes the SIRAP object (or the spatial seurat object)
(`object`), the features to plot (`features`) (if length(features) > 1, then the function will
return a list or patchwork of plots instead of just one), an assay (`assay`) and layer
(`layer`) and images (`images` - usually leave as null because we're just doing one image at a
time), image scale (`image.scale` (hires or lowres)), we can swap coordinates (`swap_coords` -
set TRUE for Visium and FALSE for HD, has to do with the structure of Visium spatial data),
feature colors (`feature_colors` - first entry is low color second is high), the zero 
tolerance - the value at which expression below is called 0 and isn't shown in the plot 
(`zero_tol`), `point_size` and `point_alpha`, whether or not we want points with highest 
expression on top (`order_points` - default TRUE), `image.alpha`, `zoom` (default FALSE) which
refers to whether or not we want to zoom in the spatial plot to focus on the nonzero regions 
only, `combine` (default TRUE) which will make it so that multiple plots are combined if 
the number of features is >1, and `title` (default NULL) which sets a title for the one/many plots. 

We can also plot multiple genes expression at the same time with `spatialExpressionBlendPlot()` and `spatialExpressionMultiPlot()`.

`plotReceptors()` is basically the same, but you can pass an airr tsv dataframe to receptors if
you don't pass a sirap object. It also requires a `group_col` argument, which is a column to
group on (like clone_id, receptor_type, etc.), and a `values` argument, which is the value in
that column to plot (defaults to all values). All other arguments are the same, but with the
addition of `receptor_legend_title`(default NULL) and `show_receptor_legend` (default TRUE),
which both do exactly what you'd think.

```{r basic-spatial-plots}
gex_plot <- spatialExpressionPlot(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  title = "AICDA expression"
)
gex_plot

features <- c("AICDA", "AIRE")
blend_plot <- spatialExpressionBlendPlot(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  features = features,
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  point_size = 0.6,
  only_blended = TRUE #if false shows individual plots of gex too
)
blend_plot

multi_plot <- spatialExpressionMultiPlot(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  features = features,
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  point_size = 0.6
)
multi_plot

all_bcr_plot <- plotReceptors(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  group_col = "receptor_type",
  values = "BCR",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  receptor_size = 1.5,
  receptor_alpha = 0.5,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  title = "All BCR-positive spots"
)
all_bcr_plot

gex_bcr_plot <- plotReceptorsExpression(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  group_col = "receptor_type",
  values = "BCR",
  feature = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  colors = "#0072B2",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  receptor_alpha = 0.8,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  title = "AICDA expression and BCR-positive spots"
)
gex_bcr_plot

demo_clone_id <- "635" # one of bigger clones
clone_plot <- plotReceptors(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  group_col = "clone_id",
  values = demo_clone_id,
  colors = "#D55E00",
  receptor_size = 1.8,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  title = paste("BCR clone", demo_clone_id)
)
clone_plot
```


# Add an analysis to the SIRAP object - cell-type deconvolution

Add the cell2location cell-type deconvolution results from the Figure 3
analysis to the SIRAP object. Here I use the normalized proportion table, which
has one row per spatial barcode and one column per cell type.

```{r attach-cell2location-results}
cell2location_path <- file.path(
  thymus_dir,
  "cell2location_analysis/results/thymus_slice2/cell2location_proportions.csv"
)

cell2location_proportions <- read.csv(
  cell2location_path,
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Need it in the right format to addMetaData
rownames(cell2location_proportions) <- cell2location_proportions$barcode
cell2location_proportions$barcode <- NULL
cell2location_proportions <- cell2location_proportions[
  colnames(spatialObject(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Use update spatial to add the cell type proportions to the sirap object
mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- updateSpatial(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  SeuratObject::AddMetaData,
  metadata = cell2location_proportions
)

spatialObject(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)@meta.data %>%
  select(`GC B`, Tfh, `Conventional CD4`, `Naive/activated B`) %>%
  summary()
```

# (Global) Moran's I and local Moran's I

Recall that Moran's I (aka global Moran's I) is a measure of spatial autocorrelation, defined 
as 
$$I\ =\ \frac{N}{S_0} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{i,j}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})} {\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2} $$, 
where $i,j$ index spatial locations, $N$ is the total number of locations, $S_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{i,j}$, $w_{i,j}$
is the weight for locations $i$ and $j$ - by default $w_{i,j} = 1$ if $i\sim j$ and is
otherwise $0$.  Moran's I values range from -1 (perfect dispersion) to +1 (perfect
correlation), with 0 indicating a random spatial pattern.

Local Moran's I, often referred to as LISA (local indicators of spatial association) offers a 
local measure of spatial autocorrelation. 
$$I_i\ =\ \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{m} \sum_{j=1}^N (x_j -\bar{x})$$, 
where $m = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{N}$, and $j$ indexes the neighbors of $i$. 
Everything else is the same as for global Moran's I. Also note that 
$$I = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{I_i}{S_0}$$,
assuming the weights used are based on neighborhood.

Our `spatialMoran()` function computes Moran's I for a given feature or metadata column in the 
sirap object. Arguments are `object` for the SIRAP object (or a spatial Seurat object), 
`variable` for the feature/clone/metadata/etc. to compute Moran's I for, 
`variable_type`(`feature`, `metadata`, `receptor`, or `clone`) for the type of variable (we can
computer Moran's I for binary data, i.e., clone presence, but it's suggested to examine a join 
count statistic instead), `value` is an optional argument used to specify a positive value (1) 
for converting a character variable (i.e., if we have variable = "sirap_receptor_type", 
variable_type = "metadata", value = "BCR" to set 1s in the spots where the value of 
sirap_receptor type = "BCR" and 0s in the spots where that isn't the case), `barcode_col` and 
`clone_col` can be specified if needed, and if they aren't then they get pulled from the sirap 
object (if possible), `layer` is the assay layer to use for features and `images` is the same 
if we have multiple images in the spatial object, `image.scale` and `swap_coords` are the same 
as earlier, `radius` is a distance by which to define neighbors for the weight in the Moran's I
calculation, if `radius` is not used, `k` is the number of nearest neighbors to use in a knn 
way, and `alternative` is the alternative hypothesis for the Moran's I test. The function 
returns a list with `test`, which contains the Moran's I statistic, expected value, variance, 
z-score, and p-value, `weights`, which contains the weight matrix used for the calculation 
layer, `data`, `neighbors`, `radius`, `k`, and `variable`.

`spatialLocalMoran()` is the same, but it computes local Moran's I for each spot and returns a dataframe that includes, among other things, the `local_i`, `expected_i`, `variance_i`, `z_i`, `p_value`, and `k` for each spot.  It's also better to plot in space with 
`plotSpatialLocalMoran()`.

```{r morans-i}
aicda_moran <- spatialMoran(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  variable = "AICDA",
  variable_type = "feature",
  layer = "data",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  k = 6
)
aicda_moran$test

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- setAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "morans_i",
  list(AICDA = aicda_moran)
)
```

```{r local-morans-i}
aicda_local_moran <- spatialLocalMoran(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  variable = "AICDA",
  variable_type = "feature",
  layer = "data",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  k = 6
)

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- setAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "local_morans_i",
  list(AICDA = aicda_local_moran)
)

aicda_local_plot <- plotSpatialLocalMoran(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  aicda_local_moran,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  title = "AICDA local Moran's I"
)

plot(aicda_local_plot)
```

# Ripley's cross K

Recall that Ripley's cross K is a measure of spatial correlation for two distinct point types, 
call them type $A$ and type $B$.
$$K(r)\ =\ \frac{1}{N_A N_B} \sum_{i=1}^{N_A} \sum_{j = 1}^{N_B} I(d_{i,j} \leq r)$$, 
where $r$ refers to the length of a radius, $N_A$ is the total number of points of type $A$ in
the population and $N_B$ is the total number of points of type $B$ in the population, $d_{i,j}$
is the distance between points $i$ and $j$, $I(d_{i,j} \leq r)$ is an indicator function that 
is 1 if the distance between points $i$ and $j$ is less than or equal to $r$ and 0 otherwise, 
and $A_i(r)$ is the area of the disc around point $i$. Essentially, this tells us if we see 
more points of type $B$ within a radius $r$ of points of type $A$ than we would expect by 
random chance.

Let's say that a spot contains a cell type when its cell2location proportion is greater than 
10%. Let's find out if Tfh cells are significantly closer to GCBs than we would expect by 
chance at any given radius. Below we get points in the right format. It's a bit weird when we 
have spots with multiple types, but the overlap is only two spots, so we'll just ignore them.

```{r ripley-marks}
mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- updateSpatial(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  function(spatial) {
    spatial$gc_b_present <- spatial$`GC B` > 0.10
    spatial$tfh_present <- spatial$Tfh > 0.10
    spatial$ripley_gc_b_tfh_mark <- dplyr::case_when(
      spatial$gc_b_present & !spatial$tfh_present ~ "GC B > 10%",
      spatial$tfh_present & !spatial$gc_b_present ~ "Tfh > 10%",
      spatial$gc_b_present & spatial$tfh_present ~ "GC B > 10% and Tfh > 10%",
      TRUE ~ "none"
    )
    spatial
  }
)

table(
  spatialObject(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)$ripley_gc_b_tfh_mark
)
```

`spatialRipleyCrossK()` is the function to call Ripley's K. It takes a SIRAP object (or spatial Seurat object) in `object`, the spatial metadata column that has the labels for the types (or marks) in `mark_col`, the two types to compare in `i` and `j`, the number of simulations to run in `nsim`, and the maximum radius to consider in `max_r`. We can also determine the cross K value for a specific radius by specifying `r`. The function works by setting the spatial window, setting up spatstat point processes with the x/y values and the marks, then running kcross and envelope from spatstat. It returns a list with the observed K, the simulated K (envelopes), data for plotting, etc.

```{r ripley-cross-k}
gc_b_tfh_k <- spatialRipleyCrossK(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  mark_col = "ripley_gc_b_tfh_mark",
  i = "GC B > 10%",
  j = "Tfh > 10%",
  nsim = 99,
  max_r = 500
)
str(gc_b_tfh_k)

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- setAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "ripley_gc_b_tfh",
  gc_b_tfh_k
)

withAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "ripley_gc_b_tfh",
  plotRipleyCrossK,
  title = "Ripley's cross K: GC B-cell and Tfh-containing spots"
)
```

# Join count for one B-cell clone

The join-count statistic examines spatial autocorrelation in binary or categorical data. It 
works by counting the number of neighboring pairs of spots that are both positive for a given 
clone. The null hypothesis is that the observed number of neighboring pairs is no different 
than what would be expected by chance. Pretty much all of the arguments are the same as in the 
Moran's I functions, but we can restrict the join count analysis to a particular polygon (or 
set of polygons) if we want. The function returns a summary table `summary`, raw `spdep` tests 
`tests`, `data` if requested (return_data = TRUE), and `neighbors`, `weights`, `k`, the 
alternative hypothesis `alternative`, and the minimum number of barcodes a clone needs to be 
found in to be tested (can run this on multiple clones at once) `min_barcodes`. Be sure to return the data if we want to plot the results with `plotSpatialCloneJoinCount()`. The plot shows all the locations with the clone and the observed and expected values of the statistic (just counts number of clone-clone neighbors).

```{r clone-join-count}
join_count_clone_id <- "635"

clone_join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount(
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  clone_ids = join_count_clone_id,
  min_barcodes = 3,
  k = 6,
  alternative = "greater",
  return_data = TRUE,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords
)

clone_join_count$summary

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- setAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "clone_join_count",
  clone_join_count
)

# withAnalysis() can inspect or summarize a stored result without removing it.
withAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "clone_join_count",
  function(result) result$summary
)

plotSpatialCloneJoinCount(
  join_count = clone_join_count,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  clone_id = join_count_clone_id,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  show_neighbors = TRUE
)
```

# Select or load GC polygons

These polygons already exist because I can't really knit the vignette with calling the Rshiny app, but I can still show how it works. The `selectSpatialPolygons()` function takes a SIRAP object `object`, an `assay` and `layer` to use for plotting, a `feature` to show on the plot (i.e., AICDA), the `image.scale` and whether or not to swap coordinates `swap_coords`, a save path to save the polygon vertices, and arguments for the Rshiny app (`host`, `port`, `plot_image`, `launch.browser`). The function returns a dataframe with the polygon vertices. If the save path already exists, it will load the polygons from that file instead of launching the Rshiny app.

`selectSpatialPolygons()` is an interactive Shiny helper for drawing region boundaries on a 
spatial Seurat/SIRAP object. At a high level, it pulls the tissue coordinates from the spatial 
object, optionally swaps/scales them using the same `image.scale` and `swap_coords` conventions
as the other SIRAP spatial functions, and opens a clickable plot of the spots. You can color 
the spots by a `feature`, optionally show the histology image underneath, adjust point 
size/opacity, and then click around the boundary of a region. Each click is snapped to the 
nearest actual spatial barcode. As you click, the function records the selected barcode, x/y 
coordinates, polygon ID, and image name. `Close polygon` repeats the first point at the end of 
the current polygon, `New polygon` closes the current one and starts another region, and the 
`remove/reset` buttons let you fix mistakes. When you hit `Done`, it closes any open polygon, 
returns a vertex table, and optionally writes that table to CSV if save_path is provided. That 
returned CSV/table is then reusable in downstream functions like polygon plotting, 
polygon-aware clone summaries, Moran/join-count calculations restricted to regions, and so on.

```{r load-or-select-polygons}
polygon_path <- file.path(
  thymus_dir,
  "plots/gc_clonal_dominance/mg_thymus_slice2",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons_vertices.csv"
)

if (file.exists(polygon_path)) {
  mg_thymus_slice2_polygons <- fread(polygon_path) %>% as.data.frame()
} else {
  mg_thymus_slice2_polygons <- selectSpatialPolygons(
    object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
    assay = "alra",
    layer = "data",
    feature = "AICDA",
    image.scale = image_scale,
    swap_coords = swap_coords,
    save_path = polygon_path,
    host = "0.0.0.0",
    port = 8788L,
    plot_image = TRUE,
    launch.browser = TRUE
  )
}

plotSpatialPolygons(
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  polygon = mg_thymus_slice2_polygons,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  polygon_alpha = 0.2
)
```

# Clonal dominance 

One of the really interesting things we can do with spatially resolved BCR/TCR data is to 
examine which clones dominate particular regions. We do this with `spatialCloneDominance()`, 
which determines which clones are in which polygon and what proportion they make up. For each 
polygon, it sums receptor counts by clone, calculates each clone’s proportion of the regional 
receptor total, attaches optional V-gene/family/superfamily summaries, and returns a list with 
the summary table and the underlying regional barcodes, coordinates, BCRs/TCRs included, 
polygon vertices, and metadata needed for downstream plotting functions.

We pass the function either a SIRAP or spatial Seurat object in `object`, if we don't pass a 
SIRAP object we should pass the spAIRR data to `receptors`. Pass the polygon vertices (the 
output from `selectSpatialPolygons`) to `polygon`, and `polygon_col`, `x_col`, and `y_col` 
should be the names of the various columns in the `polygon` dataframe. If we only want to use 
particular polygons instead of all present polygons in the `polygon` dataframe, we can pass 
those IDs to `polygon_id`. `barcode_col`, `clone_col`, `locus_col`, `count_col`, and 
`v_call_col` are all arguments to point to those columns in the spAIRR data. If `count_col` is 
NULL (which it is by default), each receptor row counts once. `locus` restricts the analysis to
specific receptor loci, and `exclude_singletons` removes singleton clones. `images`, 
`image.scale`, and `swap_coords` control which spatial coordinates are used, just as in every 
function. `include_boundary` (TRUE/FALSE - default TRUE) determines whether or not we count 
sequences on a polygon bounadry as inside or outside and `require_closed` (TRUE/FALSE - default
TRUE) determines whether or not we require the polygon to be closed (i.e., first and last 
vertex are the same) (if FALSE the polygons will be closed automatically. The function returns 
a list with `dominance`, which is a dataframe with the clone proportions, `polygons`, which is 
a dataframe with the polygon vertices, and `metadata`, which is a list with the sample ID and 
other metadata.


```{r clonal-dominance}

gc_clonal_dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  polygon = mg_thymus_slice2_polygons,
  locus = "IGH",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  exclude_singletons = TRUE
)

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- setAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "gc_clonal_dominance",
  gc_clonal_dominance
)

# updateAnalysis() applies a function to one stored result and saves the result
# back under the same name. Here I add the sample identifier to its metadata.
mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- updateAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "gc_clonal_dominance",
  function(result, sample_id) {
    result$metadata$sample_id <- sample_id
    result
  },
  sample_id = sample_id
)

withAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "gc_clonal_dominance",
  function(result) result$dominance
) %>%
  arrange(polygon, desc(proportion)) %>%
  group_by(polygon) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)

str(gc_clonal_dominance)
```

We can then plot the dominance results, and every function requires the dominance result 
(`dominance`) and the SIRAP object (`object`).  `plotSpatialRegionReceptors()` just plots a 
scatter plot with points colored to represent the top n (`top_n`) most present values in the 
`color_by` column. We also pass `image.scale`, `swap_coords`, and `images` as in all plots. 
Other arguments include `polygon_id` to restrict the plot to a particular polygon, 
`point_size`, `point_alpha`, `polygon_alpha`, `polygon_color`, `polygon_fill`, and 
`image_alpha`, all of which I think are self-explanatory. Lastly, we have `other_label` to 
determine what to call the points that don't fit into the `top_n` categories of `color_by`, 
`other_color` forr their color, `plot_other` for whether or not we want to plot them, `zoom` 
(default FALSE) in case we want to zoom in on where we have points instead of looking at the 
whole tissue, and `combine` if we want to combine separate plots if we have multiple images in 
our object. 

`plotSpatialPolygonPies()` is a cooler function that allows us to highlight the polygons and 
then either have pie charts to the side that show dominance with `mode`="side-by-side", or clip
the pie charts into the polygons with `mode`="spatial_clipped". The arguments are the same as 
in `plotSpatialRegionReceptors()`, but we also have `fill_by` (instead of color_by) to 
determine what to fill the pie charts with, `label_top_n` to determine how many of the top 
values in `fill_by` to label (things can get messy if this is too high), and `label_size` to 
determine the size of those labels. `pies_per_page` defaults to 6, and that controls how many 
pie charts are shown per page in the side-by-side mode.  If we have more than `pies_per_page`, 
we loop onto a second page.  We also have `spatial_legend` (default FALSE) which shows a shared
fill legend for `spatial_clipped` pie plots.  This is super messy so I don't really recommend 
it. Honestly, the side-by-side plots are a more useful visual, but the spatial_clipped plots 
are super fun. Both were pretty annoying to make, shout out codex for doing almost all of that 
work.

```{r clonal-dominance-spatial-plots}
gc_clone_plot <- plotSpatialRegionReceptors(
  dominance = gc_clonal_dominance,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  color_by = "clone_id",
  top_n = 20,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  point_size = 1.2,
  polygon_alpha = 0.08
)

gc_v_gene_plot <- plotSpatialRegionReceptors(
  dominance = gc_clonal_dominance,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  color_by = "v_gene_family",
  top_n = 20,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  point_size = 1.2,
  polygon_alpha = 0.08
)

gc_clone_plot
gc_v_gene_plot
```

```{r clonal-dominance-pies}
gc_clone_pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = gc_clonal_dominance,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  fill_by = "clone_id",
  mode = "side_by_side",
  top_n = 10,
  label_top_n = 5,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords
)

gc_v_family_pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = gc_clonal_dominance,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  fill_by = "v_gene_family",
  mode = "spatial_clipped",
  top_n = 10,
  label_top_n = 1,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords
)
gc_clone_pies
gc_v_family_pies

```

We can also make 3D density plots but not in the vignette.  They're pretty janky but also 
pretty fun.

```{r clonal-dominance-3d, eval=FALSE}
plotSpatialCloneDensity3D(
  dominance = gc_clonal_dominance,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  polygon_id = unique(gc_clonal_dominance$polygons$polygon)[1],
  top_n = 10,
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  plot_type = "density",
  show_polygon = TRUE,
  as_widget = TRUE
)
```

# Build and plot trees

We'll grab some of the dominant clones from the above plot and build trees for them.

```{r build-trees}
tree_clone_ids <- c("249", "295", "472")

tree_path <- file.path(walkthrough_dir, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr_trees.rds")

if (!file.exists(tree_path)) {
  imgt_refs <- dowser::readIMGT(
    file.path(hunter_dir, "germlines/imgt/human/vdj")
  )

  tree_input <- mg_thymus_slice2_sirap$receptors %>%
    filter(clone_id %in% tree_clone_ids)

  tree_input <- dowser::createGermlines(
    tree_input,
    imgt_refs,
    id = "sequence_id"
  )

  f_clones <- dowser::formatClones(
    tree_input,
    id = "sequence_id",
    germ = "germline_alignment",
    traits = "barcode_10x"
  )

  bcr_trees <- dowser::getTrees(
    f_clones,
    nproc = 1
  )

  saveRDS(bcr_trees, tree_path)
} else {
  bcr_trees <- readRDS(tree_path)
}

mg_thymus_slice2_sirap <- setAnalysis(
  mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  "trees",
  bcr_trees
)

listAnalyses(mg_thymus_slice2_sirap)
```

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` takes dowser trees and makes matched tree/spatial plot pairs for 
each clone. For a given clone, it pulls the tree, matches tree tips back to the clone data 
using tip IDs and then assigns colors to these sequences using `assignTipColors()` (which just 
assigns individual colors to each distinct tip), draws the colored lineage tree with ggtree, 
and then plots the colored tips onto the tissue image as a scatter plot. The output is a named 
list by clone ID; each clone contains a tree plot and a spatial_clone plot. Tips that exist in 
the tree but do not have matching spatial barcodes can still appear in the tree panel, but only
spatially matched tips appear on the tissue plot.

The arguments are `trees` which is just dowser `getTrees` output, `object` which is a SIRAP 
object or spatial Seurat object (if a SIRAP object isn't provided then provide `barcode_col`. 
which is the name of the column in the trees$data@data). `clone_ids` is an optional argument 
saying only plot these clones. `id_col` identifies the data column matching tree tip labels, 
and `clone_col` identifies the clone ID column. `color_by` controls how we color the tips, 
"identity" gives each tip its own color, or we could provide another column (perhaps v_call) to
color by. `palette` is an optional color palette, the default is the 32 color panel `glasbey` 
from the `pals` package (if we need >32 colors we start averaging them). `image.scale`, 
`swap_coords`, `images`, and `zoom` are all the same as usual. `tree_layout` (default 
rectangular) is passed to ggtree, as are `tree_tip_size`, and `treescale`, which all do exactly
what you'd think to the tree (how big are tips, how big is the scale bar). `spatial_tip_size` 
and `spatial_tip_alpha` adjust the scatter plot over the tissue, `order_points` does as well by
placing lower value `color_by` groups on the bottom, and `show_spatial_legend` adds a legend to
the spatial clone panel. We also have `nproc`, and `...` passes extra arguments through to 
`plotSpatialColorTips()` (which makes the scatter plot over the tissue). We can save these 
trees with `spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF()` (see below), and we mimic what the saved trees look 
like with the cowplot in the below chunk.

```{r plot-tree-spatial-pairs}
tree_spatial_pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  bcr_trees,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  clone_ids = tree_clone_ids,
  id_col = "sequence_id",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  treescale = 0.01,
  zoom = FALSE
)

first_tree_clone <- names(tree_spatial_pairs)[1]
cowplot::plot_grid(
  tree_spatial_pairs[[first_tree_clone]]$tree,
  tree_spatial_pairs[[first_tree_clone]]$spatial_clone,
  ncol = 2,
  rel_widths = c(1.2, 1)
)
```

We also have a function that groups tips into clusters based on different clustering methods, `clusterTreesTips()`. This just parallelizes over `clusterTreeTips()` for convenience. We cluster tips by (if `method = "split_largest_subtrees"`)
* Start with the full tree as one connected component
* For i in 1:k-1
* find all current connected tree components
* For each current component, calculate its genetic span as the largest patristic distance between any two tips in that component
I * Pick the current component with the largest genetic span. If tied, prefer the component with more tips
* We'll cut a branch in that component
* If cut_terminal_edges = FALSE, first consider only internal branches, only cut one of those unless no usable ones are left
* Among valid candidate cuts (two subtrees have tips), choose the cut that maximizes the size of the smaller daughter subtree (by number of tips). If two cuts tied, choose the one with longer branch length
* Cut
* i -> i+1

If `method = "cut_largest_branches"`, we just cut the longest branches in the tree until we have `k` clusters, which will minimize within group patristic difference.  Unfortunately, this method often fails to give a visually clean result, so the default is "split_largest_subtrees".

We can either choose the number of segments `k` ourselves or do so automatically.  Automatic choice of `k` is based on minimizing the mean within clusters pairwise patristic distance. Since this should go down with any cut, we require that the relative improvement of the mean within clusters pairwise patristic distance is at least `improvement_threshold`. Automated `k` choice will occur for each tree in the list.

The arguments to `clusterTreesTips()` are dowser trees `trees` , `k` (default "auto") the number of clusters to cut into, `id_col` which is the column in the `trees$data@data` that matches the tip labels, `cluster_col` which is the name of the new column to add with the cluster id (default "tree_cluster"), `prefix` (default "tree_cluster_") for the cluster annotations, `ignore_tips` (default "Germline") for the names of any tips we'd like to ignore in the clustering. Sometimes we want to build trees where not all of the tips are spatial, so we don't want the clustering to affect the nonspatial tips. Use `keep_col` to specify if there is a column with information that demarcates the tips we don't want to cluster, and `keep_value` for the values in `keep_col` that shouldn't be included in the cluster assignments (really they are included in clustering then the `keep_value` overrides the cluster value). As described above, `method` can be either "split_largest_subtrees" (the default) or "cut_largest_branches". When cutting branches, if `cut_terminal_edges` is FALSE (default TRUE) then we'll cut non-terminal branches first, otherwise we don't worry about it. If `k` is "auto", we also have `k_range` (default 1:8) for the numbers of clusters to try and `improvement_threshold` (default 0.1) for the minimum relative improvement in mean within clusters patristic distance to continue cutting.

```{r cluster-and-plot-tree-tips}
clustered_bcr_trees <- clusterTreesTips(
  bcr_trees,
  k = "auto",
  id_col = "sequence_id",
  cluster_col = "tree_cluster",
  method = "split_largest_subtrees",
  k_range = 2:8,
  cut_terminal_edges = FALSE
)

clustered_tree_spatial_pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  clustered_bcr_trees,
  object = mg_thymus_slice2_sirap,
  clone_ids = tree_clone_ids,
  id_col = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  image.scale = image_scale,
  swap_coords = swap_coords,
  treescale = 0.01,
  zoom = FALSE
)

first_tree_clone <- names(clustered_tree_spatial_pairs)[1]
cowplot::plot_grid(
  clustered_tree_spatial_pairs[[first_tree_clone]]$tree,
  clustered_tree_spatial_pairs[[first_tree_clone]]$spatial_clone,
  ncol = 2,
  rel_widths = c(1.2, 1)
)
```

```{r save-all-tree-pairs, eval=FALSE}

)
```
